name: Melville Castle
address: Gilmerton Road, Lasswade, Midlothian EH18 1AZ, Scotland

tagline: A Georgian mansion built on East India Company money for one of the most powerful men in 18th-century Scottish politics — with a three-tier Afternoon Tea now open to anyone, no room required

The current mansion was designed 1786–1791 by Edinburgh architect James Playfair for Henry Dundas, 1st Viscount Melville — a dominant figure in late 18th-century Scottish and British politics

description:
Melville Castle stands above the River North Esk at Lasswade, in Midlothian just south of Edinburgh, on a site with a documented history stretching back further than the current building itself. The earliest record dates to 1155, under a landholder named Galfrid de Malle, and the property passed to Sir John Ross in 1371. A persistent local tradition connects the earlier fortified house on this site to Mary Queen of Scots and her Italian secretary David Rizzio — one of several such associations that recur across Midlothian's castle landscape, reflecting the density of sites connected, whether firmly or loosely, to the queen's turbulent mid-16th-century reign.

The mansion visitors see today, however, is a distinctly later building, with origins in 18th-century commercial wealth rather than medieval nobility. Sir David Rannie, who had made his fortune with the East India Company, purchased the original estate in 1762. The property subsequently passed by marriage to Henry Dundas — Rannie's son-in-law — who would go on to become one of the most powerful and controversial figures in late 18th-century British politics, a dominant force in Scottish patronage networks and eventually 1st Viscount Melville. Dundas commissioned the Edinburgh architect James Playfair to design an entirely new castellated mansion, built between 1786 and 1791, replacing whatever earlier structure had stood on the site and giving Melville Castle its current late-Georgian form — castellated in silhouette, in the fashion of the period, without being a genuine defensive structure.

The Dundas family retained Melville Castle well beyond Henry Dundas's own lifetime, holding the property until after the Second World War. In the mid-20th century the castle took on institutional functions distinct from its origins as a private mansion, serving for a period as an army rehabilitation centre before a subsequent period of use as a hotel. That hotel use did not last indefinitely: the castle fell into disuse in the early 1980s, entering a period of decline that lasted over a decade.

The turning point came in 1993, when the Hay Trust purchased Melville Castle and undertook an eight-year restoration, returning the building to a condition suitable for reopening as a hotel in 2003. The castle has continued to evolve since then: a further renovation saw it reopen again in 2021 under the Original Collection group, refreshing the property for its current era of operation while retaining the Georgian mansion's essential character.

For visitors who don't want to book a room, Melville Castle's Brasserie restaurant and its Afternoon Tea service are both explicitly open to the public without any requirement to stay overnight. The Afternoon Tea runs from 13:00 to 16:00 and follows the traditional three-tier format, offering a mix of sweet and savoury items — a straightforward, well-established way to spend an afternoon inside a genuine Georgian mansion a short distance from Edinburgh, and a natural pairing with a visit to nearby Dalhousie Castle, which sits close by in the same corner of Midlothian and offers a similar public-facing dining arrangement in a considerably older building.

faqs.question: Can I have Afternoon Tea at Melville Castle without staying overnight?
faqs.answer: Yes. Melville Castle's Afternoon Tea, served from 13:00 to 16:00, follows the traditional three-tier format of sweet and savoury items and is explicitly open to non-residents — no room booking is required. The hotel's Brasserie restaurant is similarly open to the public for regular dining, making it possible to experience the Georgian mansion without an overnight stay.

faqs.question: Is Melville Castle connected to Mary Queen of Scots?
faqs.answer: There is a persistent local tradition connecting an earlier fortified house on this site to Mary Queen of Scots and her secretary David Rizzio, though the connection is not firmly documented in the way some other Scottish castle associations with the queen are. The current mansion dates from 1786–1791, considerably after Mary's 16th-century reign, so any historical connection would relate to an earlier structure on the same site rather than the building visitors see today.

faqs.question: Who was Henry Dundas, and why did he build Melville Castle?
faqs.answer: Henry Dundas, later 1st Viscount Melville, was one of the most powerful figures in late 18th-century Scottish and British politics, controlling extensive patronage networks and playing a major role in national government. He acquired the Melville estate through his marriage to the daughter of Sir David Rannie, an East India Company fortune-builder who had purchased the property in 1762. Dundas commissioned Edinburgh architect James Playfair to design the current castellated mansion, built between 1786 and 1791, as a residence befitting his political and social standing.
